1.problem:
A line in the plane is called sunny if it is not parallel to any of the \(x\)–axis, the \(y\)–axis, and the line \(x+y=0\).

Let \(n\ge3\) be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers \(k\) such that there exist \(n\) distinct lines in the plane satisfying both of the following:

  • for all positive integers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(a+b\le n+1\), the point \((a,b)\) is on at least one of the lines; and
  • exactly \(k\) of the \(n\) lines are sunny.

Solution 1

Consider a valid construction for \(k \ge 4\).

\[\text{Claim: One of the } n \text{ lines must be } x=1, y=1, \text{ or } x+y=n.\]

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction not. Then, the following holds:

\[\quad \text{1. } x=1 \text{ is not in our lines.}\]

Otherwise, two points with \(x=1\) are on the same line. This implies that each point with \(x\)-coordinate \(1\) must lie on distinct lines, hence there exists a bijection between the lines and points with \(x\)-coordinate \(1\). It follows with similar reasoning that:

\[\quad \text{2. Lines are bijective with points with } y \text{-coordinate.}\]

\[\quad \text{3. Lines are bijective with points } x+y=n+1.\]

Consider the points on \(x+y=n+1\) that are not \((1,n)\) or \((n,1)\). Then, because there exists a bijection, any such point must have a line through a point with \(x\)-coordinate \(1\) and \(y\)-coordinate \(1\) that are not \((1,n)\) or \((n,1)\) (otherwise \(x+y=n+1\) exists). But this cannot be possible if the point is not \((1,1)\). Since \(n \ge 3\), by the Pigeonhole Principle there must be at least \(1\) point that has to pass through this condition, hence we have proved the claim. \(\square\)

  • We can find the constructions for \(0,1,3\) easily.

Hence, remove one of the \(x=1, y=1,\) or \(x+y=n+1\) lines. We then get a valid covering for \(n-1\) with the same number of sunny lines! Thus, any possible number of sunny lines for \(n\) must be possible for \(n-1\). For \(n=3\), we have possibilities \(k=0, k=1, \text{ or } k=3\). By our induction above, we conclude that for any \(n\), the possible outcome for \(k\) is a subset of \(\{0,1,3\}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Solution 2

A Short Story Please don’t read this solution if you have already perfectly understood other solutions suggested :)) After solving this problem on my own, I LaTeXed the solution as I thought it is an original solution... It turned out to be the exact same solution as listed above :( Anyhow, hoping this would benefit others, I am just posting this :)

Finding all \(k\) for each \(n\) value will lead to the answer. Starting with \(n=3\), it is easy to see that \(k \in \{0, 1, 3\}\) are the only solutions.

Notice that for the rest of the cases, if a line is a "long line" (\(x=1, y=1, x+y=n+1\)), the case would be identical to its previous case \(n-1\). Therefore, investigating a case where no "long lines" are included will lead to a new potential value of \(k\).

Notice that each line must contain exactly one points from each long lines. However, no such case exists as most triples of dots will form a triangle. Therefore, by induction, all cases lead to \(n=3\), when \(k \in \{0, 1, 3\}\). \(\blacksquare\)

3.problem: Let \(\mathbb{N}\) denote the set of positive integers. A function \(f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}\) is said to be bonza if \(f(a)\) divides \(b^{a} - f(b)^{f(a)}\) for all positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Determine the smallest real constant \(c\) such that \(f(n) \leq cn\) for all bonza functions \(f\) and all positive integers \(n\).

4.problem:
A proper divisor of a positive integer \(N\) is a positive divisor of \(N\) other than \(N\) itself.

The infinite sequence \(a_1,a_2,\dots\) consists of positive integers, each of which has at least three proper divisors. For each \(n\ge1\), the integer \(a_{n+1}\) is the sum of the three largest proper divisors of \(a_n\).

Determine all possible values of \(a_1\).
4.solutions:
The possible \(a_1\)’s are those with \( ext{ord}_2(a_1)\) odd, \( ext{ord}_3(a_1) > ( ext{ord}_2(a_1)-1)/2\), and \(5 mid a_1\). This is straightforward to see from the following claims: For all \(k\)

\[ egin{aligned} & ext{(i): } 2|a_k \ & ext{(ii): } ext{If } 3 mid a_k ext{ then } a_{k+1} < a_k \ & ext{(iii): } ext{If } 3 mid a_k ext{ then } 3 mid a_{k+1} \ & ext{(iv): } 3|a_k \ & ext{(v): } ext{If } ext{ord}_2(a_k) \geq 2 ext{ and } 3|a_k ext{ then } ext{ord}_2(a_{k+1}) = ext{ord}_2(a_k)-2 ext{ and } ext{ord}_3(a_{k+1}) = ext{ord}_3(a_k)-1 \ & ext{(vi): } ext{If } ext{ord}_2(a_k) = 1 ext{ and } a_{k+1} = rac{a_k}{2} + rac{a_k}{m} + rac{a_k}{m'} ext{ then } m ext{ and } m' ext{ cannot both be odd} \end{aligned}\]

\( extbf{Proof of (i):}\) If \(a_k\) was odd note \(a_{k+1}\) is odd. Furthermore that \(a_{k+1} \leq rac{a_k}{3} + rac{a_k}{5} + rac{a_k}{7} < a_k\). Thus \(a_1,a_2,...\) would decrease indefinitely.

\( extbf{Proof of (ii):}\) Note \(a_{k+1} \leq rac{a_k}{2} + rac{a_k}{4} + rac{a_k}{5} < a_k\).

\( extbf{Proof of (vi):}\) If \(m\) and \(m'\) are both odd then \(a_{k+1}\) is odd, contradicting (i).

\( extbf{Proof of (iii):}\) If \(4 | a_k\) then \(a_{k+1} = rac{a_k}{2} + rac{a_k}{4} + rac{a_k}{m} = a_k rac{3m+4}{4m}\) for some \(m \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(3m+4 \equiv 1 \mod 3\) and \(3 mid a_k\), \(3 mid a_{k+1}\). Otherwise if \( ext{ord}_2(a_k) = 1\) (\( ext{ord}_2(a_k) > 0\) by (i)) then \(m\) or \(m'\) is even by (vi). WLOG say \(m' = 2l\) for some \(l\). Since \(l\) is a smaller divisor of \(a_k\) than \(2l\), apparently \(m = l\). Hence \(a_{k+1} = rac{a_k}{2} + rac{a_k}{l} + rac{a_k}{2l} = a_k rac{3+l}{2l}\). Since \(3 mid a_k \implies 3 mid l\). Thus \(3 mid a_{k+1}\).

\( extbf{Proof of (iv):}\) This follows immediately by (ii) and (iii).

\( extbf{Proof of (v):}\) \(a_{k+1} = rac{a_k}{2} + rac{a_k}{3} + rac{a_k}{4} = a_k rac{13}{12}\) as desired.

This concludes the proof of the claims. Now, its apparent \(a_1\) must be of the form \(2^x 3^y z\) where \(2,3 mid z\) and \(x,y > 0\), and that each successive term in the sequence decreases \(x\) by \(2\) and \(y\) by \(1\), until eventually \(x\) reaches \(1\) (not \(0\); that would contradict (i)). That is, \( ext{ord}_2{(a_{k_0})} = 1\) for some \(k_0\). Necessarily \(x\) is odd and \(y > (x-1)/2\) (if \(y = (x-1)/2\) then \( ext{ord}_3(a_{k_0}) = 0\), contradicting (iv)). If now \(5 \mid a_{k_0}\) then

\[a_{k_0} = rac{a_{k_0}}{2} + rac{a_{k_0}}{3} + rac{a_{k_0}}{5}\]

contradicting (vi). So \(5 mid a_{k_0}\), which is clearly iff \(5 mid a_1\) since at no point in the sequence before \(a_{k_0}\) can a term be divided by \(5\). In summary, \( ext{ord}_2(a_1)\) is odd, \( ext{ord}_3(a_1) > ( ext{ord}_2(a_1)-1)/2\), and \(5 mid a_1\). On the other hand these properties are sufficient.

~not_detriti

5.problem:
Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number \(\lambda\) which is known to both players. On the \(n\)th turn of the game (starting with \(n=1\)) the following happens:

  • If \(n\) is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number \(x_n\) such that \(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n\).
  • If \(n\) is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number \(x_n\) such that \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n\)

If a player cannot choose a suitable \(x_n\), the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.

Determine all values of \(\lambda\) for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
5.solutions:
Lemma 1: Alice can win if \(\lambda \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \ : \ \lambda \neq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), ignoring the case on equality.

Proof of Lemma 1:

An optimal play is that every odd turn, Alice chooses 0. Assume turn \(x_{2k}\). Bazza must satisfy:

\[x_2^2 + x_4^2 + \dots + x_{2n}^2 \leq 2k\]

By Cauchy-Schwarz,

\[x_2 + x_4 + \dots + x_{2k} \leq \sqrt{2}k\]

Hence on Alice’s next turn,

\[x_1+\dots +x_{2k} \leq \sqrt{2} k\] .

That is maximality. Now imagine that Bazza goes, and now it is Alice’s turn. From here, it is required \(\sqrt{2} k \leq \lambda(2k)\). We ignore the equality case (will go over in Lemma 3), so assume that \(\lambda > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Following the strategy, there is always a way for Alice to maximize her next move, specifically, by choosing \(x_{2k+1}>\sqrt{2k+2}\), from which it is required \(x_{2k+1}^2\le 2k+2\). However, Bazza would obtain \(x_{2k+1}^2>2k+2\), which is illegal. Hence, Alice wins. We will go back to the equality case in a moment.

Lemma 2: Bazza can win if \(0 < \lambda < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Proof of Lemma 2:

Firstly \(\lambda > 0\) is given via the statement \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+\). An optimal play for Bazza is to choose the maximal move. After Alice chooses \(x_{2k+1}\), it is required that \(2k+x_{2k+1}^2+x_{2k+2}^2 \leq 2k+2\), or \(x_{2k+2} \leq \sqrt{2-x_{2k+1}^2}\). Let Bazza choose \(x_{2k+2} = \sqrt{2-x_{2k+1}^2}\). On Alice’s side, that is \(x_{2k+1}+\sqrt{2-x_{2k+1}^2}\). Assume \(x_{2k+1} = t \geq 0\). Then, \(t+\sqrt{2-t^2}\). Also, \(t \leq \sqrt{2}\) to keep the fraction viable (as otherwise that implies Bazza has no viable moves and therefore loses, which is not allowed in this case). Therefore, for \(0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2}\), we request the minimum value of \(t+\sqrt{2-t^2}\). This is easy to find via geometry, the figure formed is a quarter circle in the first quadrant with points \((\sqrt{2},0)\), \((0,\sqrt{2})\). So the minimum value is \(\sqrt{2}\), hence \(t+\sqrt{2-t^2} \geq \sqrt{2} \ : \ 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2}\). There are \(k\) such pairs \(t\), hence the minimum value of the sum is \(x_1 + \dots + x_{2k} \leq k\sqrt{2}\). Alice requires \(x_1 + \dots + x_{2k} \leq \lambda(2k)\). That is, \(k\sqrt{2} \leq \lambda(2k+1)\). The smallest move that can be chosen from Alice is 0, and when she does so, \(k\sqrt{2} \leq \lambda(2k+1)\). Alice wins in this case, so assume the contrary, \(k\sqrt{2} > \lambda(2k)\). Then, \(\lambda < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) is when Bazza wins.

Lemma 3: Neither wins at the equality case:

Proof of Lemma 3:

We know that Bazza cannot win in that case from Lemma 2. Hence, we must show that Alice cannot win. This is quite trivial however. Substituting \(\lambda\) into \(\sqrt{2} k \leq \lambda(2k)\) we obtain \(k\sqrt{2} \geq k\sqrt{2}\) which is an equality. But then, if Bazza attempts her strategy, Alice could just play 0 and the same equality hits over and over and over again. Similarly, Alice could play 0, but then Bazza could attempt her strategy, hitting equality over and over again. Because neither player can attempt to steal victory, it is evident that no one would win.

2025 IMO/5:

Applying Lemma’s 1,2,3,

\[\begin{array}{c} \boxed{\begin{array}{c|c}0<\lambda<\frac1{\sqrt2}\&\text{Bazza wins}\\\lambda=\frac1{\sqrt2}\&\text{Neither wins}\\\lambda>\frac1{\sqrt2}\&\text{Alice wins}\end{array}} \end{array}\].

~Pinotation

Note: The motivation for Alice Winning is to show that no matter what she were to play she can manipulate Bazza’s movement. In addition, if Bazza were to play maximally when \(\lambda\) were minimal then he fully restricts Alice’s movement.
